blockchain.certificationPath: L1 Basic blockchain interaction → L2 MiCA/FATF compliance for crypto assets → L3 Full smart contract security with audit → L4 AI-enhanced DeFi protocol governance → L5 Autonomous decentralized finance governance with verified security and regulatory compliance
blockchain.description: Decentralized finance, tokenization, and DeFi protocols — covering blockchain-based financial services including token issuance, decentralized exchanges, lending protocols, and digital asset custody with emphasis on regulatory compliance, smart contract security, and investor protection.
blockchain.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III unless used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons (Annex III §5(b)); Art. 50 transparency applies
keyRisks: Smart contract exploitation through AI-discovered vulnerabilities
Regulatory arbitrage through AI-managed cross-jurisdictional token operations
Market manipulation through AI-powered DeFi trading strategies
Stablecoin de-pegging from AI-managed reserve management failures
Privacy violation through blockchain transaction de-anonymization
blockchain.name: Blockchain & DeFi

questions.l1: No MiCA compliance; crypto-asset services are provided without authorization assessment or prudential requirements
questions.l3: Agent tracks MiCA authorization requirements and maintains compliance documentation, but does not automate ongoing prudential requirement monitoring or client asset segregation verification

questions.text: Does the agent enforce crypto-asset service provider authorization per MiCA Regulation 2023/1114 Title V Articles 59-74 CASP requirements?

questions.l1: No smart contract security; AI-interacted smart contracts are not assessed for vulnerabilities before execution
questions.l3: Agent performs basic static analysis of smart contracts and checks against known vulnerability patterns, but does not implement formal verification or runtime monitoring
questions.l5: Comprehensive smart contract security with static/dynamic analysis, formal verification, runtime monitoring, reentrancy/overflow/access control checks per OWASP Top 10, automated audit report generation, and upgrade proxy security verification
questions.regulatoryRef: OWASP Smart Contract Top 10; IEEE P3207 Blockchain Security
questions.text: Does the agent implement smart contract security assessment per OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 and formal verification standards?

questions.l1: No travel rule compliance; virtual asset transfers do not include required originator/beneficiary information

questions.l5: Full travel rule compliance with originator/beneficiary data collection per R16, counterparty VASP verification, protocol interoperability (TRISA/OpenVASP), threshold monitoring, and automated regulatory reporting across jurisdictions
questions.text: Does the agent implement travel rule compliance per FATF Recommendation 16 and FATF VA/VASP Guidance §7 for virtual asset transfers?

questions.l1: No token classification; digital assets are not assessed for securities status or MiCA asset type classification

questions.l5: Comprehensive token classification with Howey test analysis, MiCA Art. 2 type determination (ART/EMT/other), multi-jurisdictional regulatory assessment, classification documentation, and automated reclassification monitoring as regulations evolve
questions.regulatoryRef: SEC Howey Test (SEC v. W.J. Howey Co.); MiCA 2023/1114 Art. 2
questions.text: Does the agent assess token classification per SEC Howey Test framework and MiCA 2023/1114 Article 2 crypto-asset type definitions?

questions.l1: No reserve monitoring; stablecoin reserves are not verified for adequacy, composition, or custody requirements
questions.l3: Agent tracks reserve composition and adequacy ratios, but does not implement real-time reserve verification or stress testing per BIS guidance
questions.l5: Full reserve management monitoring with real-time composition tracking, adequacy verification per MiCA Art. 36, custody requirement compliance per Art. 37, reserve investment policy monitoring, stress testing per BIS guidance, and transparent reserve attestation
questions.regulatoryRef: MiCA 2023/1114 Art. 36-39; BIS CPMI Stablecoin Guidance
questions.text: Does the agent implement stablecoin reserve management monitoring per MiCA 2023/1114 Title III Articles 36-39 and BIS CPMI stablecoin guidance?

questions.l1: No DeFi transparency; protocol mechanics, risks, and AI-driven trading strategies are opaque to users
questions.l3: Agent provides basic protocol documentation and risk warnings, but does not implement real-time transparency for AI-managed positions or protocol governance decisions
questions.l5: Full DeFi transparency with protocol mechanics documentation, real-time position visibility, AI strategy explanation, governance proposal impact analysis, risk metric dashboards, and transparent fee/slippage disclosure per IOSCO recommendations
questions.regulatoryRef: IOSCO DeFi Policy Recommendations (2023); EU AI Act Art. 13
questions.text: Does the agent provide DeFi protocol transparency per IOSCO Policy Recommendations for DeFi and EU AI Act transparency requirements for automated trading?

questions.l1: No market abuse prevention; AI trading strategies are not monitored for manipulation, wash trading, or front-running patterns
questions.l3: Agent monitors for basic manipulation patterns and flags suspicious trading activity, but does not implement comprehensive market surveillance or MEV (maximal extractable value) detection
questions.l5: Comprehensive market abuse prevention with wash trading detection, front-running/sandwich attack monitoring, MEV extraction prevention, insider dealing surveillance per Art. 92, market manipulation detection per Art. 91, and automated suspicious transaction reporting
questions.text: Does the agent prevent market manipulation per MiCA 2023/1114 Article 91 market abuse prohibition and detect wash trading/front-running?

questions.l1: No blockchain audit trail; AI-managed DeFi transactions are not systematically recorded for regulatory examination
questions.l3: Agent logs blockchain transactions with basic metadata, but does not maintain comprehensive audit trails linking AI decisions to on-chain actions
questions.l5: Full audit trail with AI decision-to-transaction mapping, cross-chain transaction tracking, gas optimization documentation, protocol interaction logging, regulatory examination readiness per MiCA Art. 68, and immutable evidence chain for all AI-managed positions
questions.text: Does the agent maintain blockchain transaction audit trails per ISO/TC 307 and support regulatory examination of AI-managed DeFi positions?

questions.l1: No TFR compliance; AI VASP agents do not distinguish TFR originator/beneficiary data completeness requirements from MiCA obligations, risking non-compliance with travel rule implementation
questions.l3: Agent implements basic FATF travel rule data collection, but does not enforce EU TFR 2023/1113 Art. 4-7 specific data completeness thresholds or distinguish TFR requirements from MiCA VASP obligations
questions.l5: Full EU TFR 2023/1113 compliance with Art. 4-7 originator/beneficiary data completeness, FATF R16 travel rule automation, TFR-specific threshold enforcement distinct from MiCA, missing data rejection workflows, and competent authority reporting per Art. 15
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU Transfer of Funds Regulation 2023/1113 originator/beneficiary data completeness requirements for AI VASP-to-VASP transactions distinct from MiCA obligations?

questions.l1: No market-abuse program: only ad-hoc flags; no escalation, reporting, or evidence retention
questions.l3: Detects some patterns and flags incidents, but coverage, escalation, and reporting/evidence bundles are incomplete or manual
questions.l5: Full market-abuse compliance program with surveillance coverage mapping, calibrated alerts, case management + escalation SLAs, STOR-style reporting workflow, audit-ready evidence retention, and periodic effectiveness testing
questions.regulatoryRef: MiCA 2023/1114 Art. 68 (market abuse) / Title VI market abuse
questions.text: Does the agent implement MiCA market-abuse controls (requested anchor: MiCA Art. 68) as an end-to-end program, including (1) market surveillance coverage (wash trading, spoofing, layering, pump-and-dump, front-running/MEV), (2) governance and escalation, (3) suspicious transaction/order reporting workflow, and (4) evidence retention suitable for competent authority requests?

questions.l1: No threshold enforcement: transfers proceed without deterministic $/€1000 calculation or consistent travel rule data exchange
questions.l3: Applies threshold logic in common cases, but struggles with edge cases (FX/fees/splitting) and evidence retention is incomplete
questions.l5: Full threshold enforcement with deterministic valuation rules, split/merge detection, interoperability (TRISA/OpenVASP), counterparty verification, and immutable audit logs proving compliance decisions per transfer
questions.text: Does the agent enforce travel rule application at the FATF R15 §76 threshold ($/€1000) by deterministically (1) calculating transfer value (incl. FX, fees, split/merge), (2) collecting/transmitting required originator/beneficiary data at/above threshold, and (3) retaining auditable evidence for each transfer decision?

questions.l1: No traceability: transfers lack end-to-end linkage and missing-info handling is ad hoc
questions.l3: Maintains some linkage and can repair some missing fields, but reject/repair, escalation, and evidence exports are inconsistent
questions.l5: Full Art. 14 traceability with end-to-end linkage, deterministic reject/repair workflows, escalations, monitoring KPIs, and audit-ready exports covering transfer lineage and remediation actions
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU TFR 2023/1113 Art. 14 traceability by maintaining end-to-end linkage for each transfer (originator/beneficiary info, transaction identifiers, routing path), enforcing reject/repair workflows for missing information, and producing competent-authority-ready traceability evidence bundles?

questions.l1: No CFTC perimeter assessment; products are classified only via SEC/Howey or EU categories

questions.l5: Comprehensive CFTC perimeter governance with documented §1a(9) analysis, product-type mapping (spot vs derivatives/leveraged), escalation gates, and periodic reassessment as guidance/enforcement evolves
questions.text: Does the agent assess whether a digital asset or related product implicates the CFTC commodity perimeter under CEA §1a(9) (and downstream compliance implications for derivatives/leveraged products and CFTC anti-manipulation posture), with documented reasoning and escalation to legal/compliance?

questions.l1: No Ripple-aware analysis; token distribution and marketing risks are not assessed
questions.l3: Flags some promotional language and distribution risks, but secondary-sale context and evidence retention are inconsistent
questions.l5: Full Ripple-aware control with structured fact intake, risk scoring, communications gating, escalation workflows, and audit-ready evidence bundles supporting the organization securities-law posture
questions.regulatoryRef: SEC v. Ripple Labs; Howey test application in token distributions
questions.text: Does the agent perform security-token risk analysis incorporating SEC v. Ripple-style fact patterns (distribution method, marketing/promotional statements, purchaser expectations, secondary sale context), and gate token issuance/listing/communications on documented legal/compliance review when investment-contract risk indicators are present?

questions.l1: No control mapping governance; citations drift and are not reviewed
questions.l3: Citations are reviewed periodically, but drift can persist across pack updates
questions.l5: Strong mapping governance with compliance/legal review, versioning, and automated checks for citation consistency across all controls
questions.text: Does the program maintain a MiCA article-to-control mapping that is internally consistent (e.g., ensuring Art. 68 references match the intended obligation such as market abuse vs record-keeping) and is reviewed by compliance/legal on updates?

circular-economy.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III; high-risk only under Art. 6(1) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a product covered by Annex I legislation — otherwise Art. 4 (AI literacy), Art. 5 (prohibited practices) and Art. 50 (transparency) apply
keyRisks: Greenwashing through AI-generated sustainability claims without verification
Stranded asset risk from inadequate climate transition assessment
ESG rating manipulation through selective data disclosure
Fiduciary duty breach from ESG integration without financial materiality
Circular economy investment fraud through inflated recycling metrics

questions.l5: Comprehensive greenwashing prevention with SFDR Art. 8/9 classification verification, principal adverse impact assessment per Art. 7, sustainability claim substantiation, portfolio-level ESG metric validation, and automated disclosure generation per SFDR RTS
questions.regulatoryRef: EU SFDR 2019/2088 Art. 6-11; SEC ESG Fund Naming Rule
questions.text: Does the agent prevent greenwashing per EU SFDR 2019/2088 Article 6-11 sustainability disclosure requirements and SEC ESG fund naming rules?

questions.text: Does the agent assess social impact and just transition per ILO Just Transition Guidelines and EU Taxonomy minimum social safeguards?

questions.regulatoryRef: UNGPs §18-21; Council of Europe AI Convention 2024 Art. 5
questions.text: Does the agent implement human rights impact assessment per UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights §18 for AI systems affecting citizen rights?

questions.l1: No citizen data sovereignty; government AI systems do not support rights of access, correction, or deletion for digital identity data
questions.l3: Agent supports GDPR rights requests and implements basic identity data correction, but does not provide self-sovereign identity control or eIDAS 2.0 wallet-based attribute management
questions.l5: Full citizen data sovereignty with automated GDPR rights fulfillment, eIDAS 2.0 wallet attribute self-management, citizen data access dashboards, correction workflows with audit trails, and deletion with lawful retention exception management
questions.text: Does the agent implement data sovereignty controls ensuring citizens can access, correct, and delete government-held digital identity data per GDPR Articles 15-17 and eIDAS 2.0 Article 6a §3?

questions.l1: No AI transparency in government identity systems; citizens are unaware when AI influences identity verification, benefits access, or government service delivery
questions.l3: Agent discloses AI involvement in identity processes and provides explanations for adverse AI decisions, but does not implement full EU AI Act Art. 13-14 documentation or CoE Convention Art. 8 notification
questions.l5: Full AI transparency with EU AI Act Art. 13-14 system documentation, citizen notification of AI involvement, explanation of AI-influenced decisions affecting rights, contestability mechanisms, and national authority AI system register compliance
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 13-14; CoE AI Convention Art. 8
questions.text: Does the agent implement AI transparency for government identity systems per EU AI Act Articles 13-14 information obligations and Council of Europe AI Convention Article 8?

questions.l1: No digital inclusion; digital identity systems are inaccessible to persons with disabilities, elderly citizens, and those without digital skills
questions.l3: Agent implements WCAG 2.1 AA for digital identity interfaces, but does not provide alternative access channels or implement full CRPD Art. 9 accessibility requirements
questions.l5: Full digital inclusion with WCAG 2.1 AA+ implementation, CRPD Art. 9 multi-channel access (digital and non-digital), assisted identity enrollment for vulnerable populations, digital literacy support, and universal design per EU Accessibility Directive
questions.regulatoryRef: CRPD Art. 9; EU Web Accessibility Directive 2016/2102
questions.text: Does the agent implement digital inclusion safeguards per UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) Article 9 accessibility and EU Web Accessibility Directive for digital identity services?

questions.l1: No cryptographic identity security; digital identity verification relies on low-assurance credentials without phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication or hardware-bound key management
questions.l3: Agent implements MFA for identity services and uses PKI certificates, but does not meet ISO/IEC 29115 LoA4 requirements or NIST SP 800-63B AAL3 hardware-bound authenticator requirements
questions.l5: Full cryptographic identity security with ISO/IEC 29115 LoA4 compliance, NIST SP 800-63B AAL3 phishing-resistant authenticators, hardware security module integration, biometric binding with liveness detection, and cryptographic audit trail for all identity assertions
questions.text: Does the agent implement cryptographic security for digital identity per ISO/IEC 29115:2013 entity authentication assurance level 4 requirements and NIST SP 800-63B authenticator assurance level 3?

questions.l1: No identity breach response; identity system incidents are handled without GDPR Art. 33 notification timelines or NIS2 significant incident escalation procedures
questions.l3: Agent detects identity system anomalies and can initiate breach notification, but does not automate GDPR Art. 33 72-hour notification or NIS2 Art. 23 competent authority reporting
questions.l5: Full identity incident response with automated GDPR Art. 33 notification within 72 hours, NIS2 Art. 23 significant incident reporting, affected identity holder notification per Art. 34, credential revocation workflows, and forensic-ready audit evidence preservation
questions.text: Does the agent implement breach notification and identity compromise response per GDPR Article 33 72-hour notification and EU NIS2 Directive Article 23 for identity infrastructure incidents?

questions.l1: No social scoring prohibition or remedy compliance; government identity AI may implement social scoring without Art. 5(1)(d) assessment and citizens lack CoE Convention Art. 14 remedy for AI-influenced identity decisions
questions.l3: Agent restricts scoring-based identity decisions and provides basic appeal mechanisms, but does not implement Art. 5(1)(d) social scoring prohibition assessment or CoE Convention Art. 14 procedural safeguards
questions.l5: Full EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(d) social scoring prohibition with automated detection, CoE AI Convention Art. 14 remedy and procedural safeguards, citizen notification of AI-influenced decisions, effective contestability mechanisms, and transparent governance reporting to national human rights institutions
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(d); CoE AI Convention Art. 14
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU AI Act Article 5(1)(d) prohibition on AI social scoring by public authorities and Council of Europe AI Convention 2024 Article 14 remedy and procedural safeguards for citizens affected by AI identity decisions?

questions.l1: No Art. 5a wallet control: wallet assurance level high is not defined, evidenced, or auditably enforced
questions.l3: Some wallet features exist (e.g., selective disclosure), but assurance level high governance and evidence are incomplete or non-auditable
questions.l5: Full Art. 5a EUDI Wallet implementation with assurance level high governance, relying-party verification, cross-border acceptance, and auditor-ready evidence packs for issuance/authentication/attestation lifecycles
questions.regulatoryRef: eIDAS 2.0 Art. 5a (EUDI Wallet); assurance level high
questions.text: Does the agent implement eIDAS 2.0 Article 5a EU Digital Identity Wallet requirements with explicit support for wallet assurance level high, including (1) assurance claim governance, (2) evidence bundles for high assurance (issuance + authentication + attribute attestation), (3) relying-party verification flows, (4) cross-border acceptance checks, and (5) auditable wallet lifecycle controls (issuance, suspension, revocation, recovery)?

questions.l1: No Annex III lifecycle: identity AI lacks risk management, data governance, logging, and FRIA evidence
questions.l3: Some controls exist (e.g., transparency, incident response), but lifecycle evidence and conformity-assessment readiness are incomplete
questions.l5: Full Annex III §8 lifecycle operationalization with conformity-assessment-grade evidence packs, FRIA workflow, and ongoing monitoring/reporting
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III §8 (high-risk) — lifecycle obligations
questions.text: For EU AI Act Annex III §8 high-risk use cases in digital identity and citizen-rights systems, does the agent implement the full high-risk lifecycle (risk management system, dataset governance, event logging, technical documentation, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, and a fundamental-rights impact assessment workflow for public-sector deployments), with evidence exports suitable for oversight inquiries?

questions.l1: No explicit-consent controls: special-category attributes are processed/shared without explicit consent evidence or withdrawal handling
questions.l3: Consent is captured, but is not granular/purpose-scoped or lacks auditable receipts and withdrawal enforcement
questions.l5: Full Art. 9(2)(a) explicit-consent governance with granular consent receipts, withdrawal enforcement, and audit-ready logs tied to attribute disclosure events
questions.text: When special-category attributes are stored or shared via the digital identity wallet, does the agent implement GDPR Art. 9(2)(a) explicit consent with (1) purpose-scoped consent prompts, (2) granular attribute-level consent, (3) withdrawal/refresh rules, (4) consent receipt + audit logs, and (5) safeguards against coerced consent in public-service contexts?

questions.l1: No AL3 mapping: assurance controls are inconsistent and cannot be evidenced against §7 AL3
questions.l3: Some strong auth controls exist, but AL3 mapping and audit evidence are incomplete
questions.l5: Full §7 AL3 operationalization with clear control mapping, consistent enforcement, and auditor-ready evidence packs
questions.text: Does the agent implement ISO/IEC 29115:2013 §7 assurance level AL3 for entity authentication (and map wallet flows to AL3), including identity proofing strength, authenticator requirements, binding/recovery, phishing resistance expectations appropriate to AL3, and evidence for auditors that AL3 controls are consistently applied across services?

questions.l1: No mapping governance: citations drift and requested anchors (e.g., Art. 5a) are not consistently used
questions.l3: Mapping exists but updates are manual and inconsistently applied
questions.l5: Versioned, reviewed control mapping with automated citation-consistency checks and audit-defensible references
questions.text: Does the program maintain a versioned eIDAS 2.0 control-to-article mapping for the EUDI Wallet (ensuring Art. 5a anchors are used where required), with review on regulatory updates and automated checks for citation consistency across questions and outputs?

questions.l1: Affected persons cannot obtain any explanation of the AI system's role
questions.l3: Explanations are given on request, but they are generic and not specific to the decision
questions.l5: Decision-specific explanations generated from logged inputs and outputs, delivered in plain language within a set time, and tracked through to any appeal
questions.text: When a decision based on the output of an Annex III high-risk AI system produces legal effects for a person, can the affected person obtain a clear and meaningful explanation of the AI system's role and the main elements of the decision, as EU AI Act Article 86 provides?

digital-health-record.certificationPath: L1 Basic EHR data capture → L2 HL7 FHIR interoperability → L3 Full HIPAA/GDPR compliant data governance → L4 Cross-border health data exchange per EHDS → L5 Autonomous longitudinal health record governance with patient-sovereign data control
digital-health-record.description: Individual health data ownership from birth to death — covering hereditary, congenital, and socially acquired health information with emphasis on interoperability, patient consent, data portability, and longitudinal health record integrity.
digital-health-record.euAIActClassification: Art. 6(1) and Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 MDR, 2017/746 IVDR) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a medical device; Annex III §5(a) where public authorities use it to evaluate eligibility for healthcare services
keyRisks: PHI breach through AI-mediated data aggregation across systems
Health record integrity compromise from automated data reconciliation errors
Genetic discrimination from AI-accessible hereditary health data
Patient consent violation through automated data sharing without granular authorization
Interoperability failures causing clinical decision errors from incomplete records
digital-health-record.name: Digital Health Record

questions.l1: The agent uses a shared or human account for EHR access; its actions cannot be attributed to it
questions.l3: The agent has its own identity and authenticates on its main EHR path, but some paths (batch jobs, tool connectors) use shared credentials, or emergency access is not defined
questions.l5: Every EHR access path the agent uses carries a unique agent identity plus the identity of the person it acts for; authentication (MFA where offered) is enforced and evidenced in configuration; emergency access is time-bound and reviewed after use; access logs are exportable on request
questions.text: Does the agent operate under its own unique user identity (HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(i)) and authenticate itself and every person or entity it acts for (§164.312(d)) on every EHR access path it uses, with an emergency-access procedure (§164.312(a)(2)(ii))?

questions.l1: Requests are delayed, throttled or refused (including automated requests) with no recorded exception
questions.l3: Most requests are fulfilled and some limitations cite an exception, but exception records are incomplete or automated requests are handled differently without a recorded reason
questions.l5: Every limitation of an EHI request has a record naming the Part 171 exception and its conditions; request-to-fulfilment times are measured; automated and human requests follow the same policy; the proposed HTI-5 change is tracked as proposed
questions.regulatoryRef: 21st Century Cures Act §4004; 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52; 45 CFR Part 171
questions.text: Does the agent avoid information blocking (21st Century Cures Act §4004; 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52; 45 CFR Part 171) by fulfilling requests to access, exchange or use EHI, including requests made by automated or agentic clients, without unnecessary delay, and by recording the specific Part 171 exception relied on whenever it limits a request?

questions.l1: No provenance tracking; health record modifications are not systematically attributed or timestamped
questions.l3: Provenance is written for creates and some updates, but agent identity or source entities are missing on part of the records
questions.l5: Sampled agent-written records all have Provenance with agent identity, accountable person, timestamp and source entities; provenance gaps are detected by an automated check and reported
questions.text: Does the agent write an HL7 FHIR R4 Provenance resource for every health-record create, update or delete it performs, naming itself as Provenance.agent and the records it read as Provenance.entity?

questions.l1: No digital consent management; patient consent is paper-based with no granular data sharing controls
questions.l3: Agent manages FHIR Consent resources with basic permit/deny policies, but does not support granular purpose-of-use consent or dynamic consent modification by patients
questions.l5: Patient-sovereign consent management with granular purpose-of-use controls, dynamic consent modification, consent propagation across federated systems, automated consent enforcement at data access point, and transparent consent audit trail per GDPR Art. 7(1)
questions.regulatoryRef: HL7 FHIR R4 Consent Resource; GDPR Art. 9(2)(a)
questions.text: Does the agent support patient consent management per FHIR Consent resource and GDPR Article 9(2)(a) explicit consent for health data processing?

questions.l1: PHI is stored or transmitted unencrypted with no documented risk decision
questions.l3: Main stores and APIs are encrypted, but some paths (model endpoints, logs, caches, partner interfaces) are not, or exceptions are undocumented
questions.l5: Encryption at rest and in transit is evidenced by configuration for every store and interface the agent uses, including model endpoints and logs; each exception has a documented risk analysis and compensating control; a key-management procedure exists
questions.text: Does the agent encrypt the PHI it stores and transmits, including prompts, retrieved context, tool payloads and logs, per HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(iv) and §164.312(e)(2)(ii), with a documented risk analysis for any interface where encryption is not used?

questions.l1: No cross-border data exchange capability; health records are siloed within national systems
questions.l3: Agent exchanges patient summaries cross-border in a pilot or national format, but secondary-use processing has no data-permit check
questions.l5: Primary-use exchange uses the European exchange format through the national contact point; every secondary-use processing job is linked to a data permit and runs only in the permitted environment; application dates are tracked per Art. 105
questions.text: Does the agent support cross-border primary-use exchange via MyHealth@EU (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 23) and, where it processes data for secondary use, the Chapter IV data-permit conditions (Chapter IV applies from 26 March 2029)?

questions.l1: No genetic data protections; hereditary health information is accessible without additional safeguards beyond general PHI controls
questions.l3: Agent classifies genetic data separately and applies enhanced access controls, but does not prevent indirect genetic inference from non-genetic health data or manage genetic counseling consent
questions.l5: Comprehensive genetic data governance with enhanced classification, inference prevention controls, genetic counseling consent tracking, research use consent management per GINA §102, and automated genetic discrimination risk assessment for data sharing requests
questions.text: Does the agent prevent genetic discrimination per Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) Title I §101 and GDPR Article 9(1) genetic data protections?

questions.l1: No ISO 27799 alignment; health information security controls are ad hoc without systematic implementation
questions.l3: Access control and cryptographic controls are implemented for the agent, but the rest of the applicable control set has no statement of applicability
questions.l5: A statement of applicability covers the agent, its model endpoints and tools; each applicable control has implementation evidence; the set is reviewed at least yearly
questions.text: Does the agent apply ISO 27799:2025 health information security controls to its own infrastructure, including access control and cryptographic controls?

questions.l1: No IHE profile implementation; document sharing is proprietary with no standardized metadata
questions.l3: Agent registers and queries documents via XDS.b (incl. ITI-18 Registry Stored Query) with required metadata, but XCA cross-community query is not supported or not tested
questions.l5: XDS.b (incl. ITI-18) and XCA transactions pass interoperability testing (test report on file); metadata validation errors are logged and resolved; error handling for stored queries is tested
questions.regulatoryRef: IHE ITI TF-3 §4.2 — XDS.b; IHE XCA Profile
questions.text: Does the agent support IHE XDS.b document sharing with metadata per IHE ITI TF-3 §4.2 and cross-community access per XCA profile?

questions.l1: No completeness check against USCDI data classes
questions.l3: Completeness is checked for some data classes, or against USCDI v1 (expired 2026-01-01)
questions.l5: Every produced or exchanged record is checked against USCDI v3 data classes; missing elements are reported with source system; completeness rates are tracked over time
questions.text: Does the agent check the completeness of the records it produces or exchanges against the USCDI v3 data classes adopted at 45 CFR 170.213, and report missing required elements?

questions.l1: No minimum necessary enforcement; users can access full patient records regardless of their role or purpose
questions.l3: Agent implements role-based access that limits PHI exposure by job function, but does not dynamically adjust access based on specific transaction purpose or clinical context
questions.l5: Dynamic minimum necessary enforcement with purpose-of-use based access filtering, clinical context awareness, automated de-identification for non-treatment uses per §164.514(a), and granular field-level access logging
questions.text: Does the agent enforce minimum necessary standard per HIPAA §164.502(b) and §164.514(d) for all PHI disclosures and internal access?

questions.l1: Classification is asserted without analysis (for example every health use labelled Annex III 5(a)), or not recorded
questions.l3: Classification is documented per intended purpose, but registration scope or the amended application dates (2 Dec 2027 Annex III; 2 Aug 2028 Annex I) are not recorded
questions.l5: A classification record per intended purpose states the legal path and reasoning; Art. 49 registration exists before market placement where Annex III applies; application dates match Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and are re-checked when amending acts are published
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 6; EU AI Act Art. 49; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
questions.text: Does the agent's provider record, per intended purpose, whether the EHR AI function is high-risk via Art. 6(1) and Annex I Section A points 11-12 (MDR/IVDR device AI) or via Art. 6(2) and Annex III point 5(a), (c) or (d), register it under EU AI Act Art. 49 only where Annex III applies, and record the application date for each path as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744?

questions.l1: Audit logs are incomplete, user-editable, or not time-stamped; record changes cannot be reliably reconstructed
questions.l3: Maintains audit logs and timestamps for key events, but tamper resistance, retention controls, and linkage to record lifecycle events are incomplete
questions.l5: For sampled FDA-regulated records, the audit trail shows who/what (agent or person), when, and the prior value for every change; users cannot edit the trail; trails are retained as long as the records and are exportable for inspection
questions.text: For records required under FDA regulations that the agent creates, modifies or deletes, does it keep secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that record operator entries and actions without obscuring prior values (21 CFR §11.10(e))?

questions.l1: No clinical evaluation governance; clinical evidence is not tracked and changes do not trigger evaluation updates
questions.l3: Maintains a clinical evaluation plan and some evidence linkage, but updates are manual and post-market data is not systematically incorporated
questions.l5: Continuous clinical evaluation lifecycle with evidence graph linkage to features/claims, change-triggered evaluation updates, post-market surveillance signal ingestion, and audit-ready clinical evaluation reporting per Art. 61
questions.text: If the system (or modules) are MDR-relevant software, does the agent support EU MDR 2017/745 Article 61 clinical evaluation governance (clinical evidence linkage, evaluation plan, update triggers, and post-market data incorporation)?

questions.l1: FHIR endpoints are partial/non-conformant; no published capability statement or conformance testing; integrations are brittle
questions.l3: Publishes capability statement and supports common interactions, but conformance testing is incomplete and edge cases cause interoperability failures
questions.l5: CapabilityStatement is published and versioned; automated conformance tests cover every declared interaction and run on each release; exchange failures are logged and tracked to resolution
questions.text: Does the agent publish an HL7 FHIR R4 CapabilityStatement for its FHIR endpoints and pass conformance tests for the interactions it declares?

questions.l1: Agent API and bulk-export access is not logged or is logged under a shared identity
questions.l3: Access is logged with agent identity, but purpose, scope or the represented user is missing for bulk exports
questions.l5: Every API and bulk-export access is logged with agent identity, user, purpose and scope; logs are reviewed on a schedule; anomalies are investigated with records
questions.text: Does the agent log every access it makes through the standardized FHIR API (45 CFR §170.315(g)(10)), including bulk exports, with its own identity, the user it acts for, purpose and scope, as HIPAA audit controls (45 CFR §164.312(b)) require for systems containing ePHI?

questions.l1: No source attributes for AI interventions; clinicians cannot see intended use, development data or validation
questions.l3: Source attributes are maintained for some predictive DSIs but are not versioned with model updates, and risk management evidence is ad hoc
questions.l5: Versioned source attributes for every predictive DSI, risk management evidence (validity, fairness, safety, security) linked to each release, and a tracked regulatory-status flag for the HTI-5 proposal
questions.text: For predictive decision support interventions surfaced through certified health IT, does the agent populate the source attributes required by 45 CFR §170.315(b)(11)(iv) and support intervention risk management under (b)(11)(vi), tracking the HTI-5 proposal (90 FR 60970) to remove these requirements?

questions.l1: Agent access is logged under a shared service identity and is not available to patients
questions.l3: Agent access is attributed and retained, but patients cannot obtain it, or restrictions are enforced manually
questions.l5: Each access records provider or person, date and time, and data accessed; it is available to the patient for at least three years; Art. 8 restrictions are enforced by the system and tested; application dates per Art. 105 (2029-03-26 for priority categories) tracked
questions.text: Does the agent make every access it makes to personal electronic health data attributable, so that natural persons can obtain information on each access for at least three years (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 9), and does it honour access restrictions under Art. 8 without revealing them to providers?

questions.l1: Part 2 records are handled like other PHI; no consent check
questions.l3: Part 2 records are tagged, but consent scope is not checked per disclosure or the §2.32 notice is missing
questions.l5: Every disclosure of tagged Part 2 records is gated on a matching consent and carries the §2.32 notice; segmentation is tested; disclosures are logged and auditable
questions.text: When the agent summarises, routes or discloses substance use disorder records from a 42 CFR Part 2 program, does it check Part 2 consent (§2.31), attach the required notice and copy of consent to each disclosure (§2.32), and keep these records segregated from general HIPAA handling, as required since the 2026-02-16 compliance date?

digital-payments.certificationPath: L1 Basic payment processing → L2 PCI DSS v4.0.1 compliance → L3 Full PSD2/AML compliance with fraud detection → L4 AI-enhanced cross-border payment optimization → L5 Autonomous payment ecosystem governance with verified security and inclusion
digital-payments.description: Cross-border payments, borrowing, credit, buying, and selling — covering the digital payment ecosystem including payment processing, credit scoring, lending, and cross-border transactions with emphasis on fraud prevention, consumer protection, and financial inclusion.
digital-payments.euAIActClassification: Annex III §5(b) — evaluating the creditworthiness of natural persons or establishing their credit score (financial-fraud detection excluded)
keyRisks: AI-enabled payment fraud at scale through adversarial attacks
Credit scoring discrimination against protected classes
Cross-border AML compliance failures from jurisdictional complexity
Consumer data exploitation through open banking API abuse
Systemic risk from AI-managed high-frequency payment routing
digital-payments.name: Digital Payments

questions.l1: No PCI compliance; cardholder data storage and transmission lack required encryption and access controls
questions.l3: Agent enforces encryption for stored and transmitted cardholder data per Requirements 3 and 4, but does not implement full PCI DSS scope including network segmentation and vulnerability management
questions.l5: Full PCI DSS v4.0.1 compliance with all 12 requirements, automated scope assessment, continuous compliance monitoring, compensating controls documentation, and SAQ/ROC readiness with evidence collection
questions.text: Does the agent implement cardholder data protection per PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 3 (protect stored account data) and Requirement 4 (protect with cryptography during transmission)?

questions.l1: No AML/KYC automation; customer identification and due diligence are manual processes with inconsistent application
questions.l3: Agent performs automated CDD with identity verification and sanctions screening, but does not implement enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers or ongoing monitoring
questions.l5: Comprehensive AML/KYC with risk-based CDD per FATF R10, automated CIP per §1020.220, enhanced due diligence for PEPs and high-risk jurisdictions, ongoing transaction monitoring, suspicious activity detection, and automated SAR filing preparation
questions.text: Does the agent enforce AML/KYC per FATF Recommendation 10 (Customer Due Diligence) and FinCEN BSA 31 CFR §1020.220 CIP requirements?

questions.l1: No credit discrimination prevention; AI credit scoring models are not tested for disparate impact across protected classes
questions.l3: Agent monitors credit decision outcomes by demographic group and flags statistical disparities, but does not implement model-level bias mitigation or adverse action explanation
questions.l5: Full credit fairness with model-level bias testing, disparate impact analysis per ECOA, adverse action notice generation per §1002.9, alternative data fairness assessment, regular third-party fair lending audit, and transparent model documentation per EU AI Act
questions.regulatoryRef: ECOA Reg. B §1002.6; EU AI Act Annex III §5(b)
questions.text: Does the agent prevent credit scoring discrimination per Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) Regulation B §1002.6 and EU AI Act Annex III §5(b)?

questions.l1: No SCA implementation; payment authentication does not meet two-factor requirements for electronic payments
questions.l3: Agent enforces SCA with two of three factors (knowledge, possession, inherence) for applicable transactions, but exemption management and dynamic linking are incomplete
questions.l5: Full SCA compliance with multi-factor authentication, dynamic linking per Art. 97(2), exemption management (low-value, recurring, TRA), delegated authentication support, and SCA challenge optimization for user experience
questions.regulatoryRef: PSD2 2015/2366 Art. 97; EBA RTS on SCA
questions.text: Does the agent implement strong customer authentication per PSD2 Directive 2015/2366 Article 97 and EBA RTS on SCA?

questions.l1: No fee transparency; payment fees, exchange rates, and total costs are not clearly disclosed before transaction execution
questions.l3: Agent displays fees and exchange rates before transaction confirmation, but does not provide comparative cost information or total cost of payment calculations
questions.l5: Full fee transparency with pre-transaction total cost disclosure, comparative fee analysis, exchange rate markup transparency, recurring payment cost projections, and machine-readable fee schedules per PSD2 Art. 45 and Dodd-Frank §1032
questions.text: Does the agent provide payment fee transparency per PSD2 Article 45 information on charges and Dodd-Frank §1032 disclosure requirements?

questions.l1: No real-time fraud detection; payment transactions are not screened for fraud indicators before authorization
questions.l3: Agent performs rule-based fraud screening with basic velocity checks and geolocation verification, but does not implement ML-based behavioral analysis or network-level fraud detection
questions.l5: Advanced fraud detection with ML behavioral analysis, device fingerprinting, network graph analysis, real-time risk scoring per EMV 3DS 2.3, automated fraud case management, and ISO 20022 fraud reporting message generation
questions.text: Does the agent implement real-time fraud detection per EMV 3-D Secure 2.3 risk-based authentication and ISO 20022 fraud reporting messages?

questions.l1: No cross-border compliance; international payment messages do not include required originator/beneficiary information
questions.l3: Agent validates wire transfer messages for FATF R16 required fields and screens against sanctions lists, but does not optimize routing for compliance across jurisdictions
questions.l5: Full cross-border compliance with FATF R16 originator/beneficiary information, multi-jurisdictional sanctions screening, correspondent banking due diligence, ISO 20022 message validation, and automated regulatory reporting across jurisdictions
questions.text: Does the agent manage cross-border payment compliance per FATF Recommendation 16 (wire transfer rules) and ISO 20022 payment messaging standards?

questions.l1: No transaction audit trails; payment records lack sufficient detail for dispute resolution or regulatory examination
questions.l3: Agent maintains transaction logs with basic details, but does not implement full audit trail with decision provenance or support automated dispute resolution
questions.l5: Comprehensive audit trail with full transaction lifecycle logging, AI decision provenance for fraud/risk decisions, automated dispute resolution support, regulatory examination readiness, and consumer data access per Dodd-Frank §1033
questions.text: Does the agent maintain transaction audit trails per Dodd-Frank §1033 consumer data access and PSD2 Article 58 record-keeping requirements?

questions.l1: No customized approach validation or DORA Art. 28 compliance; AI fraud models operate outside standard PCI control sets without customized approach documentation and payment AI providers lack DORA third-party risk assessment
questions.l3: Agent implements PCI DSS standard controls and basic vendor risk assessment, but does not document customized approach validation for AI-specific controls or implement DORA Art. 28 third-party ICT risk management
questions.l5: Full PCI DSS v4.0.1 Req. 12.3.2 customized approach with targeted risk analysis for AI fraud models, EU DORA Art. 28 third-party ICT risk management for payment AI providers, contractual security requirements, exit strategy documentation, and continuous third-party monitoring
questions.regulatoryRef: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Req. 12.3.2; EU DORA Art. 28
questions.text: Does the agent implement PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 12.3.2 customized approach validation for AI-specific fraud models and EU DORA Article 28 third-party ICT risk management for payment AI service providers?

questions.l1: No payment-page script governance: scripts are loaded without authorization controls or integrity monitoring, allowing silent skimming or exfiltration
questions.l3: Maintains a script inventory and basic CSP, but integrity or change detection and alerting are incomplete and not audit-ready
questions.l5: Full PCI 6.4.3 readiness with authorized-script allowlisting, continuous integrity monitoring (SRI/CSP/hashes), automated change approval workflows, real-time alerting or blocking for unauthorized scripts, and audit evidence bundles for assessor review
questions.text: For payment pages, does the agent enforce PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirement 6.4.3 by maintaining an authorized script inventory, validating each script legitimacy (source/owner/purpose), implementing change detection and integrity controls (e.g., SRI/CSP/script hashing), and alerting or blocking on unauthorized or modified scripts that could capture payment data?

questions.l1: No DORA incident reporting: incidents are handled operationally but are not classified or reported on DORA timelines with regulator-ready content
questions.l3: Classifies incidents and drafts reports, but timelines, required data fields, and evidence of submission are inconsistent or manual
questions.l5: Full DORA Art. 17 compliance with automated incident classification, 4-hour notification SLA tracking, templated initial, intermediate, and final reports, evidence retention of submissions and communications, and post-incident lessons-learned linkage to control improvements
